newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Anti-Mobutu campaign gathers steam in Zaire capital.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Mobutu campaign gathers steam in Zaire capital.

text.p: The campaign to topple Zaire's long-serving President Mobutu Sese Seko is expected to gather steam on Tuesday with street protests by students.
After shutting down the capital with a widely-observed stay-at-home order on Monday, Mobutu's opponents want to show they, not the cancer-stricken president, are in control.

"It is the opposition, led by Etienne Tshisekedi, that commands. If we ask people to stay at home, they stay at home. If we ask them to go on the streets, they go on the streets," opposition spokesman Laurent Mabyo told Reuters on Monday.

Former prime minister Tshisekedi is Mobutu's arch political rival. His followers have resorted to militant street action to end Mobutu's 32-year rule while Laurent Kabila's rebels pursue an armed campaign from the east of Zaire.
Kabila's forces have seized half the territory of a country the size of Western Europe and have declared Kinshasa their immediate target.
The rebels have relaunched their drive after a three-day pause to give Mobutu a chance to step down honourably. He ignored Kabila's deadline, which lapsed on Sunday.
Political analysts said the escalating campaign in Kinshasa was increasingly intended to bolster Tshisekedi's position after what is seen as an inevitable rebel takeover of the capital.
"Tshisekedi played the leading role in ending Mobutu's one- party rule. His followers want to make sure they have a role in a post-Mobutu era," one analyst told Reuters.
Pro-Tshisekedi protest organisers have asked students to skip school and college and to turn out in vehicles on Tuesday.
In the past, such protests have led to turmoil as students commandeered any vehicles on the street.
Mobutu declared a state of emergency last week, and although Moday's protest sparked no serious incidents, Information Minister Kin-Kiey Mulumba said troops would act to keep order.
"Force must be at the service of the law," the minister told a news briefing after a cabinet meeting devoted to the growing crisis.
Monday's protest closed the capital's shops, schools, and businesses. Public transport was off the streets as were most private vehicles. The business district was deserted.
Security forces were deployed heavily at potential flashpoints. Witnesses said soldiers fired in the air to disperse a crowd near Tshisekedi's home but there were no reports of major violence.
"The government here does not in any way respond to public opinion. If it were in Europe it would have already resigned," Mbayo said.
As the protest crippled the capital on Monday, Kabila entered Zaire's second city Lubumbashi in triumph to celebrate the fall of the copper capital to his forces last week.
Kabila, who earlier announced the capture of the West Kasai capital Kananga, swept into Lubumbashi to a tumultuous welcome.

With the fall of Lubumbashi, Kinshasa is the only major city still under the control of Mobutu's ragged army, which has collapsed in the face of the rebellion launched on Zaire's eastern border in October.
